scenes.title: What Are Collective Nouns
narration: Have you ever seen a big group of birds flying together in the sky?
When things come in a group, we use a special name for them.
These special group names are called collective nouns.

scenes.title: Learning The Idea
narration: Think of a crowd, a team, or even a bunch of flowers.
A collective noun names a whole group as one single thing.
Even if there are many people, we call them one team.

scenes.title: Examples From Daily Life
narration: Look at a pride of lions roaming in Gir Forest.
Or watch a school of fish swimming in a river.
Even a fleet of ships sailing across the Arabian Sea.

scenes.title: Recap And Think
narration: Collective nouns name a collection of people, animals, or things.
We use these words to describe groups as one unit.
Think about it: What would you call a group of bees?

scenes.title: What is a Noun
narration: Look around your room, what do you see?
Everything you see has a name, and those names are called nouns.
Nouns are simply naming words for people, places, or things.

scenes.title: Common vs Proper Nouns
narration: Common nouns name general things, like a boy, a city, or a river.
But proper nouns give special names to someone or something specific.
Proper nouns always start with a big capital letter.
Think of it like a secret label just for them.

scenes.title: Using Examples in India
narration: River is a common noun, but Ganga is a proper noun.
Boy is a common noun, but Rahul is a proper noun.
City is a common noun, but Delhi is a proper noun.
Notice how Rahul, Ganga, and Delhi always start with capital letters.

scenes.title: Recap and Think
narration: Common nouns are general, while proper nouns are specific.
Always remember to capitalize those special proper names.
Can you name your favorite festival and tell me if it is a proper noun?

scenes.title: The Mystery of Invisible Things
narration: Look at this apple. You can touch and see it.
But can you see or touch your happiness?
Today we will learn about abstract nouns.

scenes.title: What Are Abstract Nouns?
narration: Abstract nouns are names for ideas, feelings, and qualities.
They are things you cannot hold in your hand.
You experience them with your heart or mind.
For example, bravery is an abstract noun.

scenes.title: Spotting Them in Sentences
narration: Rohan felt joy when he won the race.
Look for the word joy in the sentence.
Priya showed great kindness to her friend.
Kindness is an idea, not a physical object.

scenes.title: Recap and Think
narration: Remember, concrete nouns are things you can touch.
Abstract nouns are feelings, ideas, and qualities.
Can you think of an abstract noun for a feeling you had today?

scenes.title: What Are Action Words?
narration: Have you noticed how much you do in one day at school?
You run, you jump, and you learn new things every single day.
These special words that show action are called verbs.

scenes.title: Verbs Make Sentences Move
narration: A sentence needs a verb to tell us what is happening.
Without a verb, your sentence would just be standing still.
Verbs are the engine that makes our sentences run.

scenes.title: Let's Spot The Verb
narration: Look at Rohan. He eats a delicious apple for his snack.
The word eats tells us exactly what Rohan is doing.
Now, look at Priya. She writes in her notebook.
The word writes is the verb because it shows her action.

scenes.title: Quick Grammar Recap
narration: Verbs are action words that show what someone or something does.
Every complete sentence must have at least one action verb.
Think about it: What three verbs describe what you do at home?

scenes.title: The Name Problem
narration: Meet Rohan, Rohan loves cricket, and Rohan plays in the park every day.
Does Rohan sound a bit repetitive when we say his name three times?
We need a secret tool to fix this, and it is called a pronoun!

scenes.title: What Are Pronouns
narration: A pronoun is a word that takes the place of a noun.
Instead of saying Rohan again, we can use the word he.
For Priya, we use the word she, and for things, we use it.

scenes.title: Let's Practice Together
narration: Look at this sentence: Rohan ate a mango because Rohan was hungry.
We replace the second Rohan with he to make it sound better.
Now it reads: Rohan ate a mango because he was hungry.
See how much smoother that sounds?

scenes.title: Quick Review
narration: Pronouns like he, she, and it help us avoid repeating names.
They make our writing and speaking much easier to understand.
Think about it: which pronoun would you use for your best friend?

scenes.title: The Mystery Action
narration: Have you ever seen Rohan playing in the park?
Sometimes one word isn't enough to tell the whole story.
How do we make our sentences sound just right?

scenes.title: Meet the Helping Verbs
narration: A helping verb works with an action verb.
Words like am, is, and are help us show time.
They help tell us when something is happening.

scenes.title: Using Them Correctly
narration: I am reading a book about India.
Rohan is eating a tasty dosa.
They are walking to the market.

scenes.title: Time to Remember
narration: Helping verbs are like friends to action verbs.
They make our sentences clear and complete.
Think about it: Can you write a sentence using 'is'?

scenes.title: The Toy Box Mystery
narration: Have you ever found a toy and wondered who it belongs to?
Today, we are learning about possessive pronouns to show ownership.
Instead of saying Rohan's toy, we can just say his toy.

scenes.title: Learning Possessive Pronouns
narration: A possessive pronoun replaces a noun to show something belongs to someone.
Common ones are mine, yours, his, hers, ours, and theirs.
They help us talk faster without repeating names all the time.

scenes.title: A Day at the Park
narration: Look at Priya with her new red cricket bat.
If the bat belongs to her, we say the bat is hers.
Rohan has a ball, and he says this ball is mine.
They share the park, so they say the park is ours.

scenes.title: Quick Review
narration: Remember, use possessive pronouns to show who owns an object.
They are short, easy words that make sentences sound great.
Think about it: Can you find three things in your room and describe them using mine or yours?

scenes.title: The Boring Sentence
narration: Imagine you see a dog in the park.
Is the dog big, small, or fuzzy?
We need special words to describe it.

scenes.title: Meet The Adjective
narration: An adjective describes a noun.
A noun is a person, place, or thing.
Adjectives tell us how things look or feel.

scenes.title: A Tasty Example
narration: Look at this red apple.
Red is the adjective here.
Now, try a sweet mango.
Sweet describes how the mango tastes.

scenes.title: Time To Recap
narration: Adjectives make our writing colorful and clear.
They always describe a noun.
Think about it: what three words describe your favorite toy?

scenes.title: Meet the Action Words
narration: Have you ever watched Arjun play cricket in the park?
He hits the ball, but how does he hit it?
Today, we learn words that tell us how actions happen.

scenes.title: What is an Adverb?
narration: An adverb is a helper word that describes a verb.
Many of these handy words end in the letters L Y.
They tell us the manner of the action.

scenes.title: Arjun's Cricket Match
narration: Arjun runs quickly to score a run.
He swings the bat loudly at the ball.
Finally, he smiles happily at his team.

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Adverbs describe verbs and often end in L Y.
They add flavor to our sentences, making them exciting.
Think about it: how do you walk to school today?

scenes.title: Spotting the Differences
narration: Look at Rohan's bag and Priya's bag on the school desk.
Rohan's bag is heavy, but Priya's bag is even heavier.
Can we describe how things compare using special words?

scenes.title: The Three Levels
narration: First is the base form, like tall.
Next is comparative, where we add 'er' to compare two.
Last is superlative, where we add 'est' for three or more.

scenes.title: Practice With Apples
narration: See this one sweet apple from the Kashmir basket.
This second apple is sweeter than the first one.
The third apple is the sweetest of them all.

scenes.title: Quick Review
narration: Remember, we use 'er' for two and 'est' for more.
These words help us describe size, weight, and quality.
Can you name three things in your room and compare them?

scenes.title: The Mystery of the Ball
narration: Rahul is playing cricket in his garden, but he just lost his ball!
Where could it be hiding in this messy yard?
To find it, we need tiny words called prepositions.

scenes.title: Learning the Little Words
narration: Prepositions tell us where things are located.
Think of them as bridge words connecting nouns to the rest of the sentence.
They show the position of one thing compared to another.

scenes.title: Finding the Cricket Ball
narration: Look, the ball is in the basket.
Wait, now it is on the table.
And now it is under the chair!
We found it by using these special words.

scenes.title: Time to Recap
narration: Prepositions like in, on, and under help us describe locations clearly.
Always look for the relationship between two objects.
Can you name three things in your room using a preposition?

scenes.title: The Magic Glue
narration: Have you ever wanted to join two short sentences into one long, exciting one?
We use special words called conjunctions to glue our sentences together.
Meet our three best friends: and, but, and or.

scenes.title: Using And, But, Or
narration: Use 'and' to add two similar ideas together.
Use 'but' to show something is different or surprising.
Use 'or' when you have a choice between two things.

scenes.title: Rohan's Snack Time
narration: Rohan eats a samosa and he drinks some lassi.
He wants a sweet jalebi but the shop is closed.
Would you like an apple or a mango, Rohan?

scenes.title: Quick Review
narration: Remember, and adds, but contrasts, and or offers a choice.
Using these words makes your writing flow smoothly like a river.
Can you write one sentence using the word but today?

scenes.title: A Match Made in Grammar
narration: Have you ever wondered why we say Ravi eats, but they eat?
Words must agree to make sense, like matching socks in the morning.
Let us learn the secret to making our sentences sound perfect.

scenes.title: The Rule of One
narration: When there is only one person or thing, the verb needs an s.
Think of it like a little gift for the solo subject.
For example, Meera walks to the park every single day.

scenes.title: The Rule of Many
narration: When there are many people, we drop the s from the verb.
It is like the group is already strong enough on its own.
So we say, The children play cricket in the field.

scenes.title: Recap and Try
narration: Remember, one needs an s, but many stay plain.
Check your subject, then choose the right verb form.
Think about it: Do you say 'The cat sleep' or 'The cat sleeps'?

scenes.title: The Mystery of Little Words
narration: Have you noticed how we use small words before nouns, like a bag or an apple?
These are called articles, and they help us talk about things clearly.
Do you wonder why we say a pen but an orange?

scenes.title: Learning A and An
narration: Use a before words that start with a consonant sound, like a ball.
Use an before words starting with vowel sounds like a, e, i, o, u.
So we say an umbrella because it starts with the sound uh.
Remember, it is all about the sound the word makes!

scenes.title: Meeting The Special Word
narration: We use the when we talk about one specific thing, like the Taj Mahal.
If you say the sun, everyone knows exactly which sun you mean.
Use the when you mention a noun for the second time too.
Like saying, I saw a cat, and the cat was orange.

scenes.title: Quick Grammar Review
narration: Use a for consonants, an for vowels, and the for specific things.
Practice these rules every day to become a great writer.
Think about it: can you find three things in your room to describe using a, an, or the?

scenes.title: What Are Talking Marks
narration: Have you ever wanted to write down exactly what your friend said?
When we write exact words, we use special punctuation called quotation marks.
They look like tiny hooks that hug the words someone says.

scenes.title: How To Use Them
narration: First, start your sentence with a capital letter.
Then, place the opening quotation marks before the first word.
Always put a comma after the speaker's name before the quote.
Finally, add the closing marks after the punctuation inside.

scenes.title: Example With Ravi
narration: Let's see how Ravi says he is hungry.
Ravi said, "I am hungry."
See how the marks hug I am hungry.
The period stays inside the closing marks.

scenes.title: Quick Review
narration: Remember, use quotation marks for the exact words spoken.
Always use a capital letter to start the quoted sentence.
Think about it: How would you write what your teacher says today?

Grammar: Simple, Continuous and Perfect.topic: Grammar: Simple, Continuous and Perfect Tenses
Grammar: Simple, Continuous and Perfect.title: Tenses Make Stories Move

scenes.title: The Time Travel Hook
narration: Have you ever wondered how we tell stories about the past, present, and future?
It is all about using the right tense to show when things happen.
Let us learn how to use simple, continuous, and perfect tenses.

scenes.title: Understanding the Three Tenses
narration: Simple tense tells us a fact or a habit, like I eat a mango.
Continuous tense shows an action happening right now, like I am eating.
Perfect tense shows an action that is already finished, like I have eaten.

scenes.title: A Day With Rohan
narration: Rohan plays cricket in the park every Saturday morning.
Look, he is running fast to catch the ball.
He has finished the game and is now going home.

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Simple shows habits, continuous shows ongoing actions, and perfect shows finished ones.
Think about it: how would you change I read a book into a perfect tense?

scenes.title: The Mystery of Sound
narration: Have you ever heard two different words that sound exactly the same?
Like the word sun, the big star in the sky, and son, a family member.
These tricky words are called homophones.

scenes.title: Understanding Homophones
narration: Homo means same and phone means sound.
They sound the same but have different meanings.
They are also spelled differently too.

scenes.title: Spotting the Difference
narration: Look at the words blue and blew.
I have a blue pen for my homework.
The wind blew the leaves away.
They sound identical but mean totally different things.

scenes.title: Wrapping Up
narration: Remember, homophones sound the same, look different, and mean something else.
Check your spelling to make sure you use the right one.
Can you think of a sentence using the words meet and meat?

Vocabulary: Synonyms and Antonyms.title: Words That Are Same Or Opposite

scenes.title: Spotting Similar Words
narration: Have you ever wondered why we have so many different words for the same thing?
Synonyms are words that mean the exact same thing, like happy and joyful.
If Rohan is fast, we can also say he is quick.

scenes.title: Opposites Are Antonyms
narration: Now, let us look at antonyms, which are words that mean the opposite.
Think of a hot cup of chai versus a cold glass of lassi.
Hot is the antonym of cold because they are totally different.

scenes.title: Learning With Examples
narration: Let us try a big house, which is the same as a huge house.
Big and huge are synonyms because the size is the same.
But a big house is the opposite of a tiny hut.
Big and tiny are antonyms because they are different sizes.

scenes.title: Quick Word Review
narration: Synonyms are same, antonyms are opposite.
Using these words makes your writing much more fun and colorful.
Can you think of a synonym for the word sad?

scenes.title: The Mystery of Missing Marks
narration: Have you ever read a sentence that was just one long, messy line of words?
Without punctuation, it is hard to know where to pause or what the writer means.
Let's learn how to use these marks to make our writing super clear!

scenes.title: The Big Three Marks
narration: A full stop marks the end of a statement, like 'Rohan eats a mango.'
A question mark asks something, like 'Where is my bag?'
An exclamation mark shows strong feeling, like 'Wow, what a beautiful Taj Mahal!'
These marks are like traffic signals for your sentences.

scenes.title: Fixing Rohan's Messy Note
narration: Rohan wrote: 'can we go to the park'
First, we add a capital letter to start: 'Can we go to the park'
Next, we add a question mark at the end.
Now it is perfect: 'Can we go to the park?'

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Remember, use full stops, question marks, and exclamation marks to guide your reader.
Always start your sentences with a capital letter too.
Think about it: how would you punctuate: 'I love living in India'?

scenes.title: The Four Sentence Types
narration: Have you ever wondered why we use different kinds of sentences when we talk?
Every sentence we say is either a statement, a question, a command, or an exclamation.
Let's learn how to spot each one in our daily conversations.

scenes.title: Statements and Questions
narration: A declarative sentence is a simple statement, like saying I like mangoes.
It ends with a period, just like a calm full stop.
An interrogative sentence asks something, like where is my school bag?
Always remember to put a question mark at the end.

scenes.title: Commands and Exclamations
narration: An imperative sentence gives a command, like please pass the water.
It tells someone what to do and ends with a period.
An exclamatory sentence shows strong feelings, like wow, what a beautiful Taj Mahal!
We use an exclamation mark to show that excitement.

scenes.title: Wrap Up and Practice
narration: Remember, statements tell, questions ask, commands order, and exclamations show feeling.
Using these four types makes your writing and speaking much more interesting.
Think about it: can you find one of each sentence type in your textbook today?

scenes.title: Spotting Hidden Words
narration: Have you ever noticed how two small words can join to make a brand new one?
Look at the word sunflower; it is made of sun and flower.
These special words are called compound words.

scenes.title: How They Are Built
narration: To make one, just take two smaller words that stand alone.
When you put school and bus together, you get schoolbus.
The new word keeps the meaning of both parts.

scenes.title: Real Life Examples
narration: Let us try with rain and coat to make raincoat.
How about foot and ball? We get a football for the park.
Even pan and cake make a yummy pancake for breakfast.

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Remember, compound words are just two words joined into one.
They help us build bigger and better sentences every day.
Can you find a compound word in your own house right now?

scenes.title: Spotting New Words
narration: Have you ever noticed how adding a few letters can change a word completely?
Look at the word happy. What happens if we add 'un' to the front?
It becomes unhappy! That little 'un' at the start is called a prefix.

scenes.title: What is a Prefix?
narration: A prefix is a group of letters we add to the beginning of a base word.
Adding a prefix creates a brand new word with a new, special meaning.
For example, the prefix 're' means to do something again, like redo.

scenes.title: Let's Practice Together
narration: Let us take the word tie. If we add 'un', it becomes untie.
Now take the word play. Add 're' to make replay.
See how 'un' means not, and 're' means to do it again?

scenes.title: Quick Review
narration: Prefixes go at the start of words to change their meaning.
Remember, 'un' means not and 're' means again.
Think about it: Can you find a word that starts with 'un' in your book today?

scenes.title: Spotting Words at Home
narration: Look at your toy box. You might call it a colorful collection.
Did you notice the word color became colorful?
How do we turn words into new ones?

scenes.title: Learning the Suffix Rule
narration: A suffix is a letter group added to the end of a word.
It changes the meaning of the root word completely.
Think of it like a train coach attached to the back.
The root word is the engine leading the way.

scenes.title: Building Words with Suffixes
narration: Take the word help and add ful to make helpful.
Now take play and add er to make player.
Finally add less to care to make careless.

scenes.title: Recap and Practice
narration: Suffixes are endings that change how words work.
They always sit at the very end of the root.
Think about it: Can you find a suffix in your storybook today?

scenes.title: The Mystery Of Double Meanings
narration: Have you ever heard a word that has two different meanings?
These are called homonyms and they can be very confusing.
Let's explore how they work in our daily conversations.

scenes.title: Understanding How Homonyms Work
narration: Homonyms are words that sound the same but mean different things.
Sometimes they are even spelled exactly the same way too.
We must look at the sentence to understand the true meaning.

scenes.title: A Bat In The Park
narration: Look at the word bat used in two ways.
Rohan swings his cricket bat to hit the ball.
A small bat flies through the night sky.

scenes.title: Time To Practice
narration: Remember, homonyms sound identical but have different meanings.
Always check the rest of your sentence for clues.
Can you think of another word that has two meanings?

scenes.title: What Are Idioms?
narration: Have you ever heard someone say it is raining cats and dogs?
It sounds silly because no pets are falling from the sky!
These special phrases are called idioms.

scenes.title: How Idioms Work
narration: An idiom does not mean exactly what the words say.
It is a secret way to express a bigger idea.
We use them to make our speaking more colourful.

scenes.title: Examples to Learn
narration: If Rohan says he is feeling under the weather, he means he is sick.
When Priya says it is a piece of cake, she means the work is easy.
If Meera says break a leg, she is wishing you good luck!

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Idioms are fun phrases that mean something different than the words suggest.
Remember to use them to add life to your stories.
Can you think of an idiom for being very happy?

scenes.title: What are wise sayings?
narration: Have you heard your grandmother say something like, Haste makes waste?
These short, clever sentences are called proverbs.
They teach us important lessons about life in just a few words.

scenes.title: How proverbs work
narration: Proverbs are like little packets of wisdom passed down through generations.
They use pictures and stories to explain things simply.
Instead of saying be careful, people say, Look before you leap.
It means think before you act so you don't make mistakes.

scenes.title: A Proverb in Action
narration: Imagine Rohan is rushing to finish his homework quickly.
He makes many mistakes and has to start all over again.
His teacher smiles and says, Haste makes waste.
Now Rohan knows that doing things slowly is better than rushing.

scenes.title: Recap and Think
narration: Proverbs are short, wise sayings that teach us good lessons.
They help us understand how to act and how to think.
Can you ask your parents for a proverb they like?

scenes.title: The Mystery Word Hunt
narration: Have you ever been reading and found a word that looks like a puzzle?
Like when Rohan reads about a giant banyan tree in his garden?
Don't stop reading! You can solve it using clues hidden in the sentence.

scenes.title: Finding the Hidden Meaning
narration: Context clues are like breadcrumbs that lead you to the meaning.
Look for words nearby that describe or explain the tricky word.
Sometimes a synonym, or a word with the same meaning, is right there.
Other times, the sentence tells you what the word does not mean.

scenes.title: Solving a Real Sentence
narration: Read this: The hungry puppy was ravenous after his long walk.
What does ravenous mean? Look at the word hungry nearby.
Since he is hungry, ravenous must mean extremely hungry!
You used the context to solve the word puzzle perfectly.

scenes.title: Time to Be Detectives
narration: Remember, check the words before and after your mystery word.
Use the hints to make a smart guess about the meaning.
Think about it: What clues would help you figure out the word 'gigantic'?

scenes.title: The Mystery of New Words
narration: Have you ever found a big word in a book and felt stuck?
Like when Rohan read his story and saw the word gigantic.
Don't worry, we have two amazing tools to help us out!

scenes.title: Using Your Dictionary
narration: A dictionary is like a map that shows you what words mean.
Look up the word in alphabetical order from A to Z.
It tells you the meaning and how to say the word correctly.

scenes.title: Using Your Thesaurus
narration: A thesaurus helps you find synonyms, which are words with similar meanings.
Instead of saying big, you can use huge, massive, or gigantic.
It makes your writing much more exciting for your readers.

scenes.title: Time to Recap
narration: Dictionaries give meanings, while thesauruses give us better word choices.
Both tools are your best friends when learning new English vocabulary.
Think about it: which word would you choose to describe a tasty samosa?

scenes.title: The Magic Of Imaginary Tales
narration: Have you ever wondered why stories about talking animals feel so real?
Fiction is a story that comes from an author's imagination.
Let us explore how to read these stories for fun.

scenes.title: How To Read Fiction
narration: First, look for the characters who act in the story.
Next, pay attention to the setting, or where it happens.
Finally, find the plot, which is what actually happens.

scenes.title: Example Story Time
narration: Imagine Rohan finds a golden key in his garden.
He uses the key to open a secret library door.
He meets a friendly dragon inside who loves reading.

scenes.title: Recap And Explore
narration: Fiction is make-believe, featuring characters, settings, and plots.
Remember to ask who, where, and what while reading.
Think about it: If you wrote a story, who would be your main character?

scenes.title: What is Non-fiction
narration: Have you ever wondered how bees make honey or how planes fly?
These real stories are called non-fiction books.
Non-fiction means the facts are true and real.

scenes.title: Finding Key Details
narration: Non-fiction books have special tools to help us learn.
Look for the index at the back to find topics.
The table of contents lists all the chapters.
Bold words are important terms you should know.

scenes.title: Reading About India
narration: Let us read about the mighty River Ganga.
The text says it starts in the Himalayas.
We see a map and a photo to prove it.
Real photos show us exactly how it looks.

scenes.title: Recap and Explore
narration: Non-fiction gives us real facts, photos, and maps.
Use the index to find what you need quickly.
What topic would you like to explore today?

scenes.title: What is a biography?
narration: Have you ever read a book about someone's real life?
A biography is a true story written by someone else.
It tells us about their childhood, work, and big achievements.

scenes.title: Why we read them
narration: We read biographies to learn from great people who lived.
They show us how people faced challenges and succeeded.
It is like taking a walk in their shoes.

scenes.title: An Indian hero example
narration: Let us look at Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam.
His biography tells how a boy from Rameswaram became a scientist.
He worked hard to build rockets for India.
He eventually became the President of India.

scenes.title: Wrapping it up
narration: Biographies are true stories about real people's lives.
They inspire us to work hard and dream big.
Think about it: If you wrote your biography today, what is the best part?

scenes.title: What is a poem?
narration: Have you ever heard words that sound like music when read aloud?
Poems are special because they use rhythm and patterns to tell stories.
Unlike stories in books, poems often paint pictures with fewer words.

scenes.title: The Ingredients of Poetry
narration: First, look for rhyming words that sound the same at the end.
Next, notice the rhythm, which is the beat of the lines.
Poems also use imagery, which helps you see things in your mind.

scenes.title: Reading a Short Poem
narration: Let us read this together: The bright sun glows, the soft wind blows.
See how glows and blows rhyme perfectly at the end?
The rhythm makes it feel like the wind is actually moving.
You can imagine the warm sun and the cool breeze right now.

scenes.title: Recap and Explore
narration: Remember, poems use rhyme, rhythm, and clear images to delight us.
Try reading your favorite poem slowly to feel its unique beat.
Think about it: If you were to write a poem about your home, what would it sound like?

scenes.title: What Are You Thinking
narration: Have you ever looked at a friend and known they were sad without them saying a word?
That is called making an inference, or reading between the lines.
It means using clues to figure out something the author did not tell us directly.

scenes.title: How To Find Clues
narration: First, look at what the text actually says on the page.
Second, think about what you already know from your own life experiences.
When you put these together, you can solve the mystery of the story.

scenes.title: A Story Example
narration: Imagine Arjun walks into the house, shivering and holding a dripping wet umbrella.
The author did not say it is raining, but look at the clues.
We know umbrellas are for rain and shivering means it is cold.
So, we infer that it is a cold, rainy day outside.

scenes.title: Time To Recap
narration: Inference is using text clues and what you know to understand the story better.
It helps you become a super detective reader.
Think about it: What can you infer if your teacher walks in with a huge smile?

scenes.title: The World of Information
narration: Have you ever wondered how to learn about tigers in India?
We use informational texts to find real answers.
These books tell us true things about our world.

scenes.title: Finding Your Way Around
narration: First, look at the Table of Contents.
It lists the chapters and where they start.
Bold words are important terms you should know.
Captions under photos explain what you see.

scenes.title: Reading About The Ganges
narration: Let us read about the mighty River Ganges.
Check the index for the word 'Ganges'.
Read the caption under the picture of the river.
The bold text tells us it flows to the sea.

scenes.title: Putting It All Together
narration: Remember to use the index and table of contents.
Always check captions and bold words for clues.
What true fact will you discover in a book today?

scenes.title: The Big Main Idea Hook
narration: Have you ever wondered how a big story idea stays standing tall?
Think of the main idea as the roof of your house.
But what keeps that roof from falling down to the ground?

scenes.title: What Are Supporting Details?
narration: Supporting details are like the strong pillars holding the roof up.
They give us facts and reasons to explain the main idea.
Without these extra details, your story would have no support.

scenes.title: Reading About Mangoes
narration: Let us read: Mangoes are the most popular fruit in India.
Detail one: They grow in many delicious varieties like Alphonso.
Detail two: People love eating them during the hot summer.
Detail three: They are used to make sweet refreshing drinks.

scenes.title: Recap And Think
narration: Remember, the main idea is the point, and details support it.
Always look for the extra facts that explain the big topic.
Think about it: Can you find three details in your favorite book today?

scenes.title: What is the Big Idea?
narration: Have you ever read a story and wondered what it is truly about?
Every story has a main idea, like a secret message hidden inside.
The main idea is the most important point the author wants to share.

scenes.title: How to Find It
narration: First, look at the title of the story for a big clue.
Next, pay close attention to the sentences that repeat often.
Finally, ask yourself what the whole paragraph is mostly talking about.
Ignore the tiny details that are just there to help.

scenes.title: Let's Practice Together
narration: Read this: Meera loves to play cricket, swim, and run in the park.
Notice how all these activities are types of exercise?
So, the main idea is that Meera enjoys exercising.

scenes.title: Wrapping Up
narration: Remember, the main idea is the heart of the story.
It connects all the little pieces together into one big picture.
Think about it: Can you find the main idea in your favorite book today?

scenes.title: The Mystery of Actions
narration: Have you ever wondered why your umbrella pops open when it starts to rain?
Every action has a reason behind it, like a puzzle waiting to be solved.
In English, we call the reason the cause and the result the effect.

scenes.title: Understanding the Rules
narration: The cause is why something happens. It is the action or event.
The effect is what happens because of that action.
Think of it like a domino line where one push starts the movement.

scenes.title: A Story in the Kitchen
narration: Rohan forgot to water his plant, so the leaves turned brown.
The cause is Rohan forgetting to water the plant.
The effect is that the plant leaves turned brown.

scenes.title: Quick Review and Challenge
narration: Remember, the cause is the why, and the effect is the what.
Look for signal words like because, so, and since to find them.
Think about it: If you drop an ice cream cone, what is the cause and effect?

scenes.title: Spotting Differences at Home
narration: Have you ever wondered why we say apples and oranges are different?
Comparing means looking for things that are the same.
Contrasting means looking for things that are different.

scenes.title: How to Compare and Contrast
narration: First, look at both items very carefully.
Second, list features like shape, color, and taste.
Third, group the traits into same or different piles.

scenes.title: Comparing Apples and Oranges
narration: Both apples and oranges are round fruits.
But apples are smooth and oranges have bumpy skin.
Apples are crunchy, but oranges are very juicy.

scenes.title: Wrap Up and Practice
narration: We compare to find similarities and contrast to find differences.
Using a Venn diagram helps us organize our thoughts clearly.
Think about it: How would you compare a bus and a train?

scenes.title: The Big Question
narration: Have you ever argued if a movie was the best or just okay?
Some things are true for everyone, but others are just what we feel.
Let us learn how to tell a fact from an opinion!

scenes.title: What is a Fact?
narration: A fact is something that is true and can be proven.
For example, Delhi is the capital city of India.
We can check this on a map or in a book.
Facts stay the same no matter who says them.

scenes.title: What is an Opinion?
narration: An opinion is what someone thinks or feels about something.
Like saying, Mangoes are the tastiest fruit in India.
You might love mangoes, but your friend might prefer apples.
Opinions use words like best, worst, or beautiful.

scenes.title: Quick Recap
narration: Facts are true for everyone, but opinions show personal feelings.
Look for proof to find a fact, look for feelings to find an opinion.
Think about it: Is 'Cricket is a fun sport' a fact or an opinion?

scenes.title: The Hook: Too Many Words
narration: Have you ever told a friend about a long movie, but made it super short?
That is called summarizing, and it is a superpower for every reader.
Let us learn how to pick the most important parts of a story.

scenes.title: The Idea: The Summary Formula
narration: First, find the main character and where the story takes place.
Next, identify the main problem that the character needs to fix.
Finally, explain how they solved it and how the story ends.
Remember to leave out the tiny, unimportant details.

scenes.title: Example: Ananya's Lost Toy
narration: Ananya lost her favorite toy doll in the busy Delhi park.
She searched under benches and asked the friendly park guard.
Finally, the guard found the doll near the rose bushes.
So, Ananya lost her doll but the guard helped her find it.

scenes.title: Recap: Practice Makes Perfect
narration: Summarizing means telling the big ideas in your own short sentences.
Use the who, what, and how to stay on track.
Think about it: What is the most important part of your favorite book?

scenes.title: Sending Love by Post
narration: Have you ever received a colorful letter from a friend or cousin?
Writing letters is a fun way to share news with your loved ones.
Today, let's learn how to write a simple, friendly informal letter.

scenes.title: Parts of a Letter
narration: First, write your address and today's date in the top corner.
Start with a warm greeting like Dear Rohan or Dear Grandma.
The body is the main part where you write your message.
Finally, add a closing like Love or Best wishes, then sign.

scenes.title: Writing to Priya
narration: Let us write to Priya who lives in Jaipur.
Dear Priya, I hope you are having fun at school.
I visited the park yesterday and saw many colorful butterflies.
With love, Ananya.

scenes.title: Summary and Task
narration: Remember, letters need an address, a greeting, a body, and a closing.
Keep your tone kind and talk just like you are chatting.
Think about it: Who would you like to write a letter to today?

scenes.title: The Hook
narration: Have you ever wanted to write a story as exciting as your favorite book?
Every great story starts with a simple idea, like a lost puppy in Delhi.
Today, we will learn the secret recipe to build your very own narrative.

scenes.title: The Three Parts
narration: First is the beginning, where we meet our characters and learn the setting.
Next is the middle, where a problem or a surprise creates a big adventure.
Finally, the ending shows how the problem is solved and the story wraps up.

scenes.title: A Story Example
narration: Let us imagine Rohan finds a mysterious key in his garden.
He tries to open an old, locked wooden chest hidden under a tree.
Inside, he finds a map that leads him to a hidden treasure!

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Remember, every story needs a clear beginning, a middle problem, and a happy ending.
Use descriptive words to make your reader feel like they are really there.
Think about it: If you found a magic key today, what would it open?

scenes.title: The Big Hook
narration: Have you ever wanted to tell a long story about your day?
Writing one long, jumbled sentence makes it hard for friends to read.
How can we organize our thoughts to make them super clear?

scenes.title: The Idea of Paragraphs
narration: A paragraph is just a group of sentences about one main idea.
It starts with a topic sentence that tells us what to expect.
Then, supporting sentences add fun details and facts.
Finally, a concluding sentence wraps everything up nicely.

scenes.title: A Concrete Example
narration: Let's write about my favorite fruit, the juicy mango.
Topic sentence: The mango is a delicious summer fruit.
Detail: It is bright yellow and very sweet.
Detail: My mother makes tasty mango lassi with it.
Conclusion: I love eating mangoes in the summer.

scenes.title: Recap and Think
narration: Remember, a paragraph needs a topic, details, and a conclusion.
Keep all your sentences focused on just one big idea.
Think about it: What is one topic you could write a paragraph about today?

scenes.title: The Magic of Description
narration: Have you ever told a friend about a delicious mango you ate?
Did you just say it was good, or did you describe it?
Descriptive writing helps the reader see exactly what you see.

scenes.title: Using Your Five Senses
narration: Good writers use the five senses to make stories come alive.
Tell us how something looks, feels, smells, tastes, or sounds.
Instead of saying the dog is big, describe its fluffy fur.

scenes.title: Let's Describe a Park
narration: Imagine you are at Lodhi Garden in Delhi on a sunny day.
Instead of saying it is nice, say the grass is soft and green.
Add that you hear the chirping of happy birds in the trees.
Now the reader can imagine they are standing right there with you.

scenes.title: Recap and Try It
narration: Remember to use sensory words to paint a picture in your writing.
Great writers show their readers the world instead of just telling them.
Think about it: how would you describe your favorite school lunch?

scenes.title: The Big Essay Question
narration: Have you ever wondered how to write a story that makes people want to keep reading?
Writing an essay is just like telling a great story about your favorite topic.
Today, we will learn how to organize our ideas into three simple parts.

scenes.title: Building Your Essay Structure
narration: First is the Introduction, where you catch the reader's attention with a fun opening sentence.
Next is the Body, where you share your facts and cool details about your topic.
Finally, the Conclusion wraps everything up and shares what you think about your topic.

scenes.title: Example: My Favorite Festival
narration: Let us write about Diwali! We start with: Diwali is the bright festival of lights.
In the body, we write: Families decorate homes with rangoli and eat yummy sweets like laddoos.
To finish, we write: I love Diwali because it brings my whole family together happily.

scenes.title: Recap and Think
narration: Remember, every essay needs a clear beginning, a middle with facts, and a strong ending.
Use your own voice and organize your thoughts to write something truly special.
Think about it: What is one topic you know so well that you could write an essay today?

scenes.title: What is a diary?
narration: Have you ever wanted to share your day with a secret friend?
A diary is a special notebook for your personal thoughts.
It is like talking to yourself on paper every single day.

scenes.title: Writing your entry
narration: Always start your entry with the current date at the top.
Greeting your diary like a friend makes it feel natural.
Use the word I to talk about what you did.
Write about your feelings or things that happened today.

scenes.title: A Day in Delhi
narration: Let us write an entry about a fun day in Delhi.
First, write the date: 20 October.
Then, write: Dear Diary, I visited the Red Fort today.
Finally, add: I felt very happy seeing the big walls.

scenes.title: Time to recap
narration: Remember, always add the date and use the word I.
Your diary is your own, so be honest and have fun.
What is one exciting thing that happened to you today?

scenes.title: A Special Message
narration: Have you ever wanted to write a letter to your principal for a school trip?
We cannot write it like a chatty note to our best friend.
Formal letters follow a special, neat order to show respect.

scenes.title: Building Your Letter
narration: First, write your name and address at the very top left.
Next, write the date and then the receiver's name and title.
Use a clear subject line to say what the letter is about.
Start with a polite greeting like Dear Sir or Madam.

scenes.title: Writing Your Request
narration: Aarav wants a new library book, so he writes clearly.
He says, I am writing to request a new history book.
He keeps it short, polite, and uses correct grammar.
Finally, he closes with Yours faithfully and his name.

scenes.title: Remember the Rules
narration: Remember to use your best handwriting and check your spelling.
Formal letters are always polite, clear, and very organized.
Think about it: who would you write a formal letter to today?

scenes.title: The Hook: Start with Ideas
narration: Have you ever imagined a dragon living in a Mumbai apartment?
Writing a story is like building a world inside your head.
What makes a story truly exciting to read?

scenes.title: The Ingredients of Stories
narration: First, you need characters who do interesting things.
Next, pick a setting, like a busy market in Delhi.
Finally, give your character a problem to solve.
The plot is just the steps they take to fix it.

scenes.title: Let's Write a Story
narration: Meet Rohan who finds a magical cricket bat.
He lives in a sunny village in Kerala.
His problem is that his team keeps losing matches.
Rohan uses the bat to hit a giant six!

scenes.title: Recap and Try It
narration: Remember, every story needs characters, a setting, and a problem.
Start with a small idea and let your imagination soar.
Think about it: Who would be the hero of your own story?

scenes.title: The Big Hook
narration: Have you ever stood in front of your class feeling nervous?
Giving a presentation is just sharing a story with friends.
Would you like to learn how to be a star speaker?

scenes.title: Plan Your Speech
narration: First, start with a greeting like Hello everyone.
Then, tell them what you are going to talk about.
Keep your points short and easy to understand.
Always end by saying thank you for listening.

scenes.title: Practice With Rohan
narration: Rohan wants to talk about his favorite fruit, the mango.
He stands tall and looks at his classmates.
He says, Hello, today I will show you a mango.
He speaks clearly and smiles at everyone.

scenes.title: Recap and Reflect
narration: Remember to greet, explain, and thank your audience.
Speak clearly and smile to feel more confident.
Think about it: What topic would you love to present to your class?

scenes.title: Hook: Making Stories Come Alive
narration: Have you ever told a story that made your friends laugh or gasp in surprise?
Stories are like maps that take our listeners on a wonderful adventure.
Today, let's learn how to tell a story that everyone wants to hear.

scenes.title: The Idea: Building Your Tale
narration: Every good story needs a beginning, a middle, and an end.
Start by introducing your character and where they are, like a park in Delhi.
Then, add a problem or a surprise to make the middle exciting.
Finally, explain how the problem was solved to reach the end.

scenes.title: Example: Rohan's Lost Cricket Ball
narration: Let's tell a story about Rohan finding his lost cricket ball.
First, Rohan was playing cricket in the garden, but he hit the ball over the wall.
Next, he searched everywhere and felt worried because it was his favorite ball.
Then, he peeked behind a big mango tree and saw his ball sitting there.
Finally, Rohan grabbed his ball and ran back to continue his game happily.

scenes.title: Recap: Becoming a Storyteller
narration: Remember, a good story has a clear start, middle, and end.
Use your voice and expressions to show how your characters are feeling.
Think about it: what is one exciting thing that happened to you today?

scenes.title: The Magic of Pictures
narration: Have you ever looked at a photo and wondered what is happening inside it?
Today, we will learn how to turn those pictures into a wonderful story.
First, we look for clues like who, where, and what they are doing.

scenes.title: Building Your Story
narration: Start by naming the people in the picture, maybe give them a fun name like Rohan.
Next, describe the setting, like a sunny park or a busy market in Delhi.
Use action words to describe what they are doing, like running or playing.
Finally, add describing words to make your sentences pop, like happy or bright.

scenes.title: A Park Adventure
narration: Imagine a picture of Priya sitting on a bench under a big banyan tree.
She is reading a colorful book while a small dog plays near her feet.
We can write, Priya is reading a book, and her brown dog is playing.
The sun is shining brightly on a beautiful, warm afternoon.

scenes.title: Wrap Up and Practice
narration: Remember to spot the characters, the place, and the actions in every picture.
Use describing words to paint a clear picture with your writing.
Think about it: If you look at a photo of your family, what story would you write?

scenes.title: The Big Idea
narration: Have you ever told a friend about a long movie in just one minute?
That is exactly what a summary is!
It captures the main points without all the extra details.

scenes.title: How To Summarize
narration: First, read the whole story carefully.
Second, pick out the most important events.
Third, write it in your own words.
Finally, keep it short and sweet.

scenes.title: Let's Practice Together
narration: Imagine a story about Rohan buying a mango at the market.
Detail one: Rohan walked to the busy market.
Detail two: He spent 20 rupees on a ripe mango.
Summary: Rohan bought a mango at the market.

scenes.title: Quick Recap
narration: A summary tells the main idea using fewer words.
Always use your own words, not the book's exact sentences.
Can you summarize your favorite book in just three sentences?

scenes.title: Why Role-Play Matters
narration: Have you ever wondered what it is like to be a shopkeeper or a doctor?
Role-play is pretending to be someone else in a specific situation.
It helps us practice speaking clearly and using kind words.

scenes.title: The Golden Rules
narration: First, listen carefully to your partner so you know how to reply.
Use a clear voice so everyone can hear you easily.
Always stay in your character's role until the scene ends.
Be polite and say please and thank you often.

scenes.title: A Trip to the Market
narration: Let us pretend we are at a vegetable stall in Delhi.
Shopkeeper: Namaste, how many fresh carrots do you need?
Customer: Namaste, I would like five carrots please.
Shopkeeper: Here you go, that will be ten rupees.

scenes.title: Recap and Reflect
narration: Remember to listen, speak clearly, and stay in character.
Role-play turns simple conversations into fun adventures.
Think about it: who would you like to be tomorrow?

scenes.title: The Classroom Chatter
narration: Have you ever tried talking in a group and everyone spoke at once?
It gets noisy, and no one can hear what you are saying.
Today, let's learn how to share ideas politely and clearly.

scenes.title: The Golden Rules
narration: First, always wait for your turn before you start speaking.
Second, listen carefully to what your classmates are saying.
Third, look at the person you are talking to.
Finally, use kind words like please and thank you.

scenes.title: A Classroom Example
narration: Rohan wants to talk about the school garden project.
He says, Excuse me, may I share my thought?
Then Priya nods and says, Please go ahead, Rohan.
Rohan speaks clearly, and everyone listens to his plan.

scenes.title: Recap and Reflect
narration: To discuss well, take turns, listen well, and stay kind.
Group discussions are great for learning new things together.
Think about it: How can you invite a quiet friend to speak?

scenes.title: The Hook
narration: Did you ever have a day so exciting you wanted to tell everyone?
Sometimes it is hard to pick the right words to describe what happened.
Let us learn how to tell a great story today!

scenes.title: The Idea
narration: First, start by saying what happened and where you were.
Next, use feelings like happy, scared, or surprised to describe it.
Finally, tell us how the story ended.
Good stories have a clear beginning, middle, and end.

scenes.title: A Concrete Example
narration: Imagine you went to a fun fair in Delhi with your friends.
You could say: I felt happy riding the giant wheel.
Then, add: We ate yummy jalebis before going home.
See? Now your friends can picture exactly what you did!

scenes.title: Recap and Think
narration: Remember to share where, how you felt, and the ending.
Using these steps makes your stories fun to listen to.
Think about it: what is one exciting thing you did this week?

scenes.title: The Big Question
narration: Have you ever been asked what you think about your favorite book or game?
Sharing how you feel is called giving an opinion.
Let's learn how to tell people our thoughts politely.

scenes.title: Using the Right Words
narration: We start by using special phrases like I think or in my view.
Saying I think helps others know it is just your perspective.
It is okay if your friends have a different opinion too.

scenes.title: Example in the Classroom
narration: Imagine your teacher asks if you like the story about Tenali Raman.
You can say, I think the story is very funny.
Or you can say, in my opinion, he is very clever.

scenes.title: Recap and Try It
narration: Remember, use I think to start your sentence.
Be kind and listen to what your friends share back.
Think about it: What is your favorite dish to eat at home?

scenes.title: The Big Stage
narration: Have you ever felt shy when standing in front of your class?
Public speaking is just sharing your story with friends.
Let us learn how to speak clearly and confidently.

scenes.title: Key Speaking Tips
narration: First, stand tall with your shoulders back.
Next, make eye contact with the people listening to you.
Speak loudly enough so everyone in the back can hear.
Always remember to smile and breathe slowly.

scenes.title: Practicing Your Speech
narration: Imagine you are telling your class about your favorite book.
Start by saying, Hello everyone, today I want to share.
Tell them three simple things you liked about the story.
Finish by saying, Thank you for listening to me.

scenes.title: You Are A Star
narration: Practice makes you a better speaker every single day.
Remember, your voice is important and worth sharing.
Think about it, what topic would you like to speak about tomorrow?
